A-GEOMETRY: Build a frame ledger for a camera point transferred through the robot base to a tool frame. Specify transform direction and distinguish points, free vectors, twists and wrenches. Reconstruct the inverse chain and verify the round-trip error. Transfer the same physical twist between frames and show that wrench–twist power is invariant under the corresponding dual transform. Carry the position and frame convention into the visual-servo lesson; explain why a correct control law with an inverted extrinsic can move in the wrong direction. Include a near-zero rotation and a noncommuting rotation pair. A consistent endpoint alone cannot establish that every intermediate frame was correct.
A-KINEMATICS: Use one reachable arm target to compare inverse-kinematics branches, then verify both branches through forward kinematics. Transfer one branch into its Jacobian and compare a small joint perturbation with the predicted Cartesian displacement. Sweep toward a singular configuration and connect the smallest singular value to commanded joint speed. Add a null-space motion and measure the residual task-space motion at finite step size. Report which results are first-order approximations and which are exact geometry. For the coupled mobile/arm example, list the frame and unit of every velocity passed between subsystems.
A-DYNAMICS: Choose a two-link configuration and derive potential energy, its gravity gradient and the inertia symmetry test. Compare static holding torque with inverse dynamics at zero velocity and acceleration. Then introduce motion and separate inertia, Coriolis, gravity and dissipation contributions. Transfer the calculated torque into a controlled plant and explain saturation-induced tracking error. Use the identification lesson to distinguish a fitted parameter from an independently excited parameter: provide regressor rank and a withheld prediction. Finally explain which energy coordinates can be influenced in the underactuated system and why a full-actuation cancellation argument does not transfer unchanged.
A-CONTROL: Trace a commanded motion through desired acceleration, applied torque, actual joint motion and endpoint error. Show where clipping invalidates ideal computed-torque error dynamics. Compare this with the contact-energy experiment: compute stored elastic energy and account for the tank before interpreting force tracking as stable interaction. In P69 retain both the contact-study outputs and executed manipulation events, explicitly identifying that the tank does not drive the jaw-force ramp. Diagnose one actuator-limited failure and one insufficient-grasp-support failure; they require different repairs. Verify return to baseline after each fault and retain control effort as well as tracking error.
A-PERCEPTION: Construct a chain from camera calibration through a projected observation, correspondence, pose estimate and robot-frame grasp target. Carry pixel, normalized-image and metre units explicitly across each interface. Use held-out reprojection to distinguish calibration fit from prediction, then test how an outlier or wrong correspondence propagates into the target. Compare a depth uncertainty result with the capture tolerance in P62 without treating them as the same statistical distribution. For range mapping, distinguish unseen, observed-free and occupied cells; show one consequence of suppressing free-space evidence. A known-association synthetic observation is not evidence of a deployed perception detector.
A-ESTIMATION: Compare covariance before and after a measurement, its innovation and the gate decision. Then remove excitation and show why increasing sample rate cannot recover a missing observable direction. Declare state normalization before comparing mixed-state information spectra or variance traces. In P53 verify that indices 5, 10, …, 80 are withheld and that sample zero is training data. Perturb only withheld measurements and demonstrate unchanged smoothed states and covariance with changed validation residual. Distinguish deterministic coverage of a chi-square threshold from statistical consistency over independent realizations. Connect a false association to estimator bias even if the filter reports small covariance.
A-SLAM: Solve the P51 joint graph and retain both pose headings and estimated landmark coordinates. Remove the gauge prior, construct the three planar rigid-motion directions and show their null residual effect. Align gauges before comparing maps; do not interpret an arbitrary absolute offset as relative-map failure. Link the P50 one-to-one association and P52 loop-closure checks to the factors they would supply, recording where those studies remain separate. Compare the smoothing holdout result with graph fit error. In the mobile capstone identify the actual known-cell occupancy and direct-position filter interfaces; it does not execute the full joint SLAM graph, so its successful route cannot be used as an end-to-end SLAM acceptance test.
A-PLANNING: Compare graph, sampling and kinodynamic representations using the same distinction between geometric feasibility and executable motion. Retain a path cost, continuous segment clearance and terminal velocity rather than only a success flag. Demonstrate the finite-lattice no-plan case at acceleration 3 m/s² and speed 1 m/s, explaining why the first positive lattice edge is excluded without proving continuous-space impossibility. Connect P68 waypoints to its bounded-acceleration tracker and compare the planned route with actual position. Use an obstacle crossing to separate prediction from a frozen obstacle assumption. State the discretization, horizon and footprint boundaries of every clearance claim.
A-AUTONOMY: Construct a state/event trace with preconditions, success guards, failure exits and recovery actions. In P64 force the first carry route to fail, show the blacklisted edge and compare the replacement route; then exhaust both alternatives and retain explicit failure with finite elapsed time. Contrast this with P62, where transfer cannot begin before grasp verification. For the multi-agent contract, identify whose state or intent is stale and how a locally valid plan can violate a shared constraint. No restart should erase the causal event that triggered recovery. Provide one counterexample to treating an action label as proof that its physical precondition occurred.
A-MANIPULATION: Carry an estimated object pose through IK, actual joint dynamics, geometric capture, friction support, attachment offset, transfer and release. Derive the two-jaw support threshold μ = 0.220725 at 10 N per jaw for the 0.45 kg object. Compare a missed grasp with insufficient support and verify that neither carries the object. During successful transfer, check that object position equals actual endpoint plus the captured offset; after release it remains on the ideal support while the arm retreats. Relate this bounded support test to the broader force-closure lesson without equating them. Discuss omitted finger geometry, slip, contact impulses and collision checking before making a hardware claim.
A-SAFETY: Build a timing ledger separating source stamp, remote stamp, arrival order, data age, watchdog detection, hold and checkpoint resume. Derive P67 recovery duration from the event pair, and identify a censored broken run where recovery was never observed. Compare this with P68: requesting zero velocity does not instantly stop the actual plant. Record residual motion during braking and minimum clearance. Inject a timing fault, show the first monitor that detects it and identify any unmonitored interval. Distinguish bounded fallback in these synthetic models from certification, fault coverage over all hazards, physical stopping distance and real network deadline guarantees.
A-CAP-MOBILE: Submit a stage ledger linking observation → occupancy odds → route → estimated state/covariance → acceleration command → actual trajectory → freshness hold/resume. Record the numerical quantity and units passed at each arrow. At baseline, identify the occupancy threshold crossing, actual detour, hold interval, resumed motion, final error and continuous clearance. Increase dropout alone and explain covariance growth and braking. Change obstacle speed alone and determine whether it intersects the arrival interval or is inactive in that regime. In broken mode show that arrival can coexist with collision. Compare the original ideal-segment component study with the tracked extension; neither runs P51 full SLAM or models a finite vehicle footprint. Acceptance requires the bounded stage claims, not merely a green goal flag.
A-CAP-MANIP: Submit a stage ledger linking camera point → transformed target → IK → saturated torque → actual endpoint → grasp verification → attached object → placement → release/retreat. Retain all event times and the object trajectory. Independently verify the gravity/support inequality, one forward-kinematics point and final object error. Sweep visual perturbation and friction separately, identify compensation of a captured offset, and demonstrate both missed-grasp and insufficient-support failures without transfer. Keep P69 scalar contact/tank and timing checks alongside this sequence but explicitly mark them as separate component studies rather than claiming their state drives the jaw or arm. Explain the ideal supported release and omitted contact/slip/3D closure assumptions; no hardware or learner competence is inferred.
